newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Top Russian ministers accused of corruption.
newsitem.headline: Top Russian ministers accused of corruption.

text.p: The Russian government faced a growing crisis on Tuesday as media run by powerful businessmen who backed Boris Yeltsin's re-election campaign rounded on top ministers, accusing them of corruption over state asset sales.

Boris Nemtsov, the young reformer and possible presidential contender, was singled out for attacks after Friday's sale of part of the state telephone company. He hit back at his critics, accusing them of "bandit capitalism" and "blackmail by media".
Yeltsin, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Nemstov's fellow first deputy premier Anatoly Chubais, had yet to react.
Kremlin sources, however, said containing the feuding was the top priority for the government and especially for Chubais, the powerful economic reform chief who ran Yeltsin's campaign.
The row has destroyed any semblance of solidarity among the group of businessmen who quietly rallied their media muscle and money behind Yeltsin to prevent a communist victory last July.

Insiders say their reward was state assets, notably oil companies, at knock-down prices. But relations among the rival business groups have steadily worsened, with several disputes over murky state auctions ending up in the courts.

Most worrying now for ministers, one political source said, was that so many big banking and media interests seemed to be lining up against the government in pursuit of their feud with banker and former minister Vladimir Potanin. He led the group that won the quarter stake in the Svyazinvest telecoms group.

Nemtsov, in an interview published on Tuesday by a newspaper in which Potanin has a stake, said the government was determined it would no longer share out "free assets" among the "group of seven bankers". Some of them could therefore try to force him from office, he said, or cut a deal with the opposition.
"They are going to fight us with all they have. Right up to us having to quit," Nemtsov told Komsomolskaya Pravda.
"The interests of some finance-media groups could merge with the interests of the communists and fascists," he added. "A new configuration is emerging...The situation's fairly dangerous."

Nemtsov, 37, was summoned by Yeltsin to clean up government and the economy in March following the cabinet reshuffle that saw Potanin, 36, step down after just eight months in government and return to running Uneximbank, the country's third biggest.

"When I started work, the president and I agreed...there would be no more bandit capitalism," Nemtsov told reporters in the central city of Cheboksary on Tuesday. "We will take a civilised path and will hold honest sales of state assets."

Nemtsov said Potanin's group, backed by nearly $1 billion from U.S. financier George Soros, won the Svyazinvest stake fairly with the highest bid but the losers had wanted a backroom carve-up on the cheap. Soros told the Financial Times it was Nemtsov's arrival that persuaded him to invest more in Russia.

Senior political sources say the losing consortium, which included Spanish telecoms group Telefonica, was effectively run by Russian tycoons Vladimir Gusinsky, who controls NTV television and Sevodnya newspaper, and Boris Berezovsky.

Berezovsky said he suspended his business interests when Yeltsin named him to the Kremlin Security Council last December. His empire includes Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily and a large stake in ORT television, in which the state also owns 51 percent.
ORT, NTV, Nezavisimaya and Sevodnya have carried bitter attacks on Potanin, Nemtsov and privatisation minister Alfred Kokh, a long-serving liberal who is a close ally of Chubais.
NTV said unnamed bankers were using privatisations to raise funds for a presidential campaign by Nemtsov in the year 2000.

A senior government source said Chubais, who has been more directly involved in privatisation than Nemtsov, rejected pleas from Berezovsky and Gusinsky to be awarded the Svyazinvest stake. "Chubais told them those days are over," the source said.
The media have yet to attack Chubais, however. He is seen as a kingmaker at the next election, but not a candidate himself.
The economic outcome of the latest row is far from clear.
Several other big privatisations are coming up, including 38 percent of Norilsk Nickel, one of the world's biggest metals producers. Uneximbank will auction it for the government.
At a political level, one Kremlin source even forecast that Nemtsov might be deliberately put in a tight spot by his Kremlin allies to test his mettle as a possible presidential candidate.
